title: How Free Speech Works
summary: Josh and Chuck give an overview of free speech in the United States, covering the First Amendment's text and Enlightenment roots, the expansion of what counts as speech (symbolic acts, flag burning, refusing the pledge, Facebook likes), and the courts' role in shaping it. Key cases discussed include Schenck v. United States and Holmes's clear and present danger test, the Vietnam-era "F the draft" jacket case, Miller v. California and the three-prong obscenity test, Jenkins v. Georgia (Carnal Knowledge), the Child Online Protection Act (COPA), Hustler v. Falwell (Larry Flynt), Brandenburg v. Ohio on incitement, and the Innocence of Muslims video. They contrast US protections with European hate speech laws, cover group libel, blasphemy laws ending in 2007, the libel standard, and the idea that free speech does not mean freedom from consequences. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about the "would you rather" question of forgoing eating, sleeping, or breathing.

segments.title: Opening banter and overview of free speech
segments.summary: Hosts open with off-topic banter about replacing hollow doors, then introduce US free speech protections under the First Amendment, its Enlightenment and anti-British-monarchy roots, and the idea that courts have shaped free speech over time.

segments.title: Expanding the definition of speech and freedom not to speak
segments.summary: Courts have treated symbolic acts such as T-shirts, billboards, flag burning and refusing the pledge as speech. The hosts explain that free speech protects expression regardless of offense and describe the marketplace of ideas rationale.

segments.title: Group libel and hate speech versus European approaches
segments.summary: The hosts describe past US group libel laws, how they were exploited against civil rights leaders, and contrast the US with European bans on hate speech and Holocaust denial, which stem from the totalitarian past.

segments.title: Schenck case and Holmes's clear and present danger test
segments.summary: Discussion of Schenck v. United States (1919), in which material opposing the draft was held unprotected, the 'yelling fire in a theater' remark, and Holmes's later dissent that narrowed the test to clear and present danger.

segments.title: Offensive speech, unavoidable exposure and the F the draft jacket case
segments.summary: The hosts argue that the ability to look away is key to whether speech can be restricted, using skywriting as an example, and cite a Vietnam-era case where a man wearing an F the draft jacket was found protected.
topics: Cohen v. California style jacket case

segments.title: Miller v. California and obscenity test
segments.summary: Marvin Miller's mass mailings led to the Supreme Court's Miller v. California decision, which set the three-prong obscenity test using community standards. The hosts criticize the Court's role in judging obscenity and quote Hugo Black, and note the lack of a national standard.

segments.title: Jenkins v. Georgia, COPA and the Internet
segments.summary: The Carnal Knowledge theater case (Jenkins v. Georgia) found the film not obscene. The hosts then discuss the Child Online Protection Act, which was struck down in litigation partly because parental controls were an alternative and the community standard was too broad.

segments.title: Libel, satire, Hustler v. Falwell and blasphemy laws
segments.summary: The hosts cover libel as narrow unprotected speech requiring falsity and malice, satire and parody protection in Hustler v. Falwell, the Innocence of Muslims video, and US blasphemy laws that ended in 2007, along with Westboro Baptist Church.

segments.title: Freedom of speech versus consequences and the case for hate speech protection
segments.summary: The hosts discuss that free speech does not mean freedom from consequences, cite Garrett Epps and Noah Feldman, and close the argument with Jonathan Rauch's idea that refuting hateful speech publicly beats suppressing it.

segments.title: Listener mail: would you rather forgo breathing, eating or sleeping
segments.summary: Listener Andrew poses a would-you-rather question about giving up eating, sleeping, or breathing without discomfort. The hosts respond, and they also share updates about a former intern applicant and an actress guest.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and point to social media and the website for more information.
